title: Ultrasonic Sensor Characterisation & Reversing Alarm
short_description: Characterising the noise, range and beam angle of an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor in MATLAB, then applying it to a simulated car reversing alarm.
full_description: A coursework study characterising the real-world performance of the low-cost HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor against its datasheet, then applying the sensor to a practical proximity-warning application: a simulated car reversing alarm with real-time data smoothing and a MATLAB GUI.
motivation: The HC-SR04 is a low-budget ultrasonic sensor widely used in hobbyist and prototype systems, but its real-world accuracy, range limits and beam angle aren't always intuitive from the datasheet alone. The goal was to characterise it properly, then prove it out in a realistic application.
methodology: Noise characteristics were measured across a range of distances using 500-sample datasets, smoothed with a conv() moving-average filter and fitted with a linear regression model (fitlm()) to validate accuracy against manually measured distances. Minimum and maximum detection range were found by moving a barrier until the sensor stopped registering, repeated five times per condition, and the sensor's field of view was mapped by sliding a barrier along lines at known distances and using trigonometry to calculate the cutoff angle. Finally, the sensor was wired to an LED through a breadboard and driven by MATLAB to simulate a car reversing alarm, with blink rate tied to measured distance and a GUI toggle for real-time smoothing.
results: The sensor showed increasing noise at greater distances but high accuracy at short range (0.200m measured vs 0.2m true distance). Measured max/min range averaged 4.03m and 0.022m against a 4m/0.02m datasheet spec, and measured beam angle converged toward the datasheet's 30° as distance increased (35.2° at 0.2m, down to 30.3° at 0.6m). The reversing-alarm simulation successfully varied LED blink rate with distance, holding the LED solid below 0.2m to mimic a critical-proximity alarm.
lessons_learned: Beam-angle accuracy was worse at close range than far range, the opposite of what might be assumed for a proximity sensor — a reminder to characterise sensors across their full operating envelope rather than assuming datasheet figures hold uniformly. Reducing the sensor's dead zones further would need either a sensor array with overlapping beams or beamforming, both of which trade off field of view for accuracy.
